title: Storage and indexes
summary: Match the store to the access path; say what an index costs on writes.

parts.rule: Choose storage from concrete reads, writes, transactions, and data size—not from a product name. Relational storage fits related rows and transactional updates; key-value fits direct key access; object storage fits large opaque files. Every secondary index is another ordered structure maintained on writes, so name the exact query it serves and the write and space cost it adds.
parts.why: A database cannot optimize an access path that has not been defined. Missing indexes turn frequent reads into full scans, while speculative indexes consume memory, storage, and write I/O. Composite index order also matters: an index that contains the right columns in the wrong order may not support the filter and sort the application actually performs.
parts.example: A shortener has 100,000,000 link rows. Redirect uses SELECT destination_url FROM links WHERE code = ?, so code as the primary key already provides the needed lookup; another index on code is redundant. The owner dashboard runs WHERE owner_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Add a composite index on (owner_id, created_at DESC), allowing the database to seek to owner 42 and read the newest 20 entries in order. An index on created_at alone would still scan many owners, while owner_id alone may require sorting all of that owner's rows. Each create now updates both the primary-key structure and this secondary index, and each delete or owner change updates it too. Measure whether that write cost is acceptable at the estimated rate. A boolean index on disabled_at alone is often low-selectivity and may not help; include it only if the real query and distribution justify it. If each link also has a 5 MB preview image, put image bytes in object storage and keep an object key plus metadata in the relational row. That keeps ordinary link transactions and indexes small. Start with one store when it meets the paths; add a specialized time-series or search store only for a workload the primary cannot serve well.
parts.use: List the highest-volume queries before selecting a store. For each proposed index, write the filter, join, and order-by columns it supports, check column order, and account for write amplification and storage. Put large immutable blobs in object storage while keeping authoritative metadata and ownership in the transactional system.
parts.refuse: Do not add indexes for hypothetical or rare queries without measuring scan cost. Avoid multi-megabyte blobs in hot transactional rows and avoid five databases when one proven store fits. “The database will handle it” is incomplete without a key or index path. More indexes are not free, and a vendor category does not replace a data model.

body:
Rule. Choose storage from concrete reads, writes, transactions, and data size—not from a product name. Relational storage fits related rows and transactional updates; key-value fits direct key access; object storage fits large opaque files. Every secondary index is another ordered structure maintained on writes, so name the exact query it serves and the write and space cost it adds.

Why it matters. A database cannot optimize an access path that has not been defined. Missing indexes turn frequent reads into full scans, while speculative indexes consume memory, storage, and write I/O. Composite index order also matters: an index that contains the right columns in the wrong order may not support the filter and sort the application actually performs.

Worked example. A shortener has 100,000,000 link rows. Redirect uses SELECT destination_url FROM links WHERE code = ?, so code as the primary key already provides the needed lookup; another index on code is redundant. The owner dashboard runs WHERE owner_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Add a composite index on (owner_id, created_at DESC), allowing the database to seek to owner 42 and read the newest 20 entries in order. An index on created_at alone would still scan many owners, while owner_id alone may require sorting all of that owner's rows. Each create now updates both the primary-key structure and this secondary index, and each delete or owner change updates it too. Measure whether that write cost is acceptable at the estimated rate. A boolean index on disabled_at alone is often low-selectivity and may not help; include it only if the real query and distribution justify it. If each link also has a 5 MB preview image, put image bytes in object storage and keep an object key plus metadata in the relational row. That keeps ordinary link transactions and indexes small. Start with one store when it meets the paths; add a specialized time-series or search store only for a workload the primary cannot serve well.

[[diagram:index]]

When to use. List the highest-volume queries before selecting a store. For each proposed index, write the filter, join, and order-by columns it supports, check column order, and account for write amplification and storage. Put large immutable blobs in object storage while keeping authoritative metadata and ownership in the transactional system.

When to refuse. Do not add indexes for hypothetical or rare queries without measuring scan cost. Avoid multi-megabyte blobs in hot transactional rows and avoid five databases when one proven store fits. “The database will handle it” is incomplete without a key or index path. More indexes are not free, and a vendor category does not replace a data model.
